# 1. Basic Structure of HashMap

Internally, a `HashMap` uses an **array of buckets**.

Each bucket can store:

* one entry
* multiple entries (if collisions occur)

Simplified structure:

```java
class HashMap<K,V> {
    Node<K,V>[] table;
}
```

Each node stores:

```java
class Node<K,V> {
    int hash;
    K key;
    V value;
    Node<K,V> next;
}
```

---

# 2. Hashing Process

When you do:

```java
map.put("apple", 10);
```

Java performs these steps:

---

## Step 1: Calculate HashCode

Java calls:

```java
key.hashCode()
```

Example:

```java
"apple".hashCode() = 93029210
```

---

## Step 2: Improve the Hash

Java mixes bits to reduce collisions.

Simplified version:

```java
hash = h ^ (h >>> 16)
```

This improves distribution.

---

## Step 3: Find Bucket Index

Bucket index is calculated as:

\text{Bucket Index} = \text{hash} ; & ; (n - 1)

Where:

* `n` = array size
* `&` = bitwise AND

Example:

```java
16 buckets
hash = 37

37 & (16 - 1)
37 & 15
= 5
```

So data goes into bucket `5`.

Two keys can produce the same bucket index.

This is called a **collision**.

Example:

```java

put("elppa", 20)
```

Both may map to same bucket.

* `hashCode()` finds bucket

# 7. Why equals() and hashCode() Both Matter

Java contract:

```text
Equal objects MUST have same hashCode
```

Example:

```java
class User {
    int id;

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return id;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return ((User)o).id == this.id;
    }
}
```

Without proper overrides:

* duplicate keys
* retrieval failures
* performance issues

## Why capacity is power of 2?

Because index calculation using:


## Is HashMap thread-safe?

No.

## Can HashMap store null?

Yes.

* One `null` key allowed

When the `HashMap` load factor exceeds `0.75`, Java performs **resizing (rehashing)** to maintain fast performance.

# 1. What is Load Factor?

Load factor determines how full the `HashMap` can get before resizing.

Default:

```java id="4mnplz"
loadFactor = 0.75
```

Threshold formula:

\text{Threshold} = \text{Capacity} \times \text{Load Factor}

Example:

```text id="g2r8lq"
Capacity = 16
Load Factor = 0.75

Threshold = 16 ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ 0.75 = 12
```

So after inserting the **13th element**, resize happens.

---

# 2. What Happens Internally?

When threshold is exceeded:

```text id="kkz72f"
size > threshold
```

Java performs:

```text id="z28h8l"
1. Create new larger bucket array
2. Double the capacity
3. Recalculate bucket indexes
4. Move all existing entries
```

This process is called:

```text id="ybw9gc"
Rehashing
```

# 7. Redistribution Optimization in Java 8

Before Java 8:

* full recalculation was common.

Java 8 optimized resizing.

When capacity doubles:

* an element either:

  * stays in same bucket
  * OR moves by old capacity offset.

Example:

```text id="7kijcu"

Element at index 3
can move to:
3 OR 19
```

```text id="lmzmbv"

```

This makes resizing faster.

It is a balance between:

| --------------- | ---------------- |
| More memory     | Less memory      |
| Faster access   | More collisions  |

`0.75` gives:

* good performance
* reasonable memory usage
* fewer collisions

* every element is visited

* nodes moved

where `n` = number of elements.

This is why occasional insertions can be slow.

Big O notation describes how the **runtime** or **space usage** of an algorithm grows as input size grows.

It measures:

```text id="07p2mv"

```

If input size is `n`, Big O tells:

* how fast execution grows
* how memory usage grows

---

# Why Big O Matters

Suppose:

```text id="jg0e5x"
10 elements ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ fast
1,000,000 elements ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ maybe slow
```

Big O helps compare algorithms for scalability.

---

# Common Complexities

| Complexity | Name         | Performance |
| ---------- | ------------ | ----------- |
| O(1)       | Constant     | Excellent   |
| O(log n)   | Logarithmic  | Very Fast   |
| O(n)       | Linear       | Good        |
| O(n log n) | Linearithmic | Efficient   |

# Binary Search Example

Instead of checking every element:


Check middle first.

# ArrayList vs LinkedList in Java

Both `ArrayList` and `LinkedList` implement JavaÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂs `List` interface, but internally they are very different.

The choice depends on:

* insertion/deletion patterns
* access patterns
* memory usage
* performance requirements

---

# Quick Comparison Table

| Feature                 | ArrayList           | LinkedList         |
| ----------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------ |
| Internal Structure      | Dynamic Array       | Doubly Linked List |
| Random Access (`get`)   | Fast O(1)           | Slow O(n)          |
| Insert at End           | Fast O(1) amortized | Fast O(1)          |
| Insert/Delete in Middle | Slow O(n)           | Faster O(1)*       |
| Memory Usage            | Less                | More               |
| Cache Performance       | Better              | Worse              |
| Traversal               | Faster              | Slower             |

*Finding position in `LinkedList` still takes `O(n)`.

---

# 1. ArrayList Internals

Uses:

```text id="5zj31u"
Resizable Dynamic Array
```

Internally:

```java id="3m0sdf"
Object[] elements;
```

---

## Visualization

```text id="uy7pk8"
Index:
0   1   2   3
[A] [B] [C] [D]
```

Elements stored continuously in memory.

---

## Advantages

### Fast Random Access

```java id="1dh18v"
list.get(2);
```

Direct indexing.

Complexity:

```text id="v6w1g3"
O(1)
```

---

## Problem with Insertions

Insert in middle:

```java id="1s42db"
list.add(1, "X");
```

Needs shifting.

Before:

```text id="7z71jg"
[A] [B] [C] [D]
```

After:

```text id="ecij7u"
[A] [X] [B] [C] [D]
```

All elements shift right.

Complexity:

```text id="nhh9az"
O(n)
```

---

# 2. LinkedList Internals

Uses:

```text id="tfe2lc"
Doubly Linked List
```

Each node contains:

```java id="j0kh0m"
class Node {
    E data;
    Node next;
    Node prev;
}
```

---

## Visualization

```text id="hzw2zl"
null ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ [A] ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ [B] ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ [C] ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ null
```

Each node linked with pointers.

---

# Advantages

## Fast Insert/Delete

If node reference already known:

```text id="u83js6"
O(1)
```

because only pointers change.

---

## Example

Insert `X` between `A` and `B`.

Before:

```text id="9lf4ll"
A ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ B
```

After:

```text id="2g0skf"
A ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ X ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ B
```

No shifting needed.

---

# Problem with Access

Accessing:

```java id="ewz4b9"
list.get(5000);
```

Requires traversal.

Complexity:

```text id="a7p31c"
O(n)
```

because nodes are not contiguous.

---

# Time Complexity Comparison

| Operation     | ArrayList      | LinkedList |
| ------------- | -------------- | ---------- |
| get(index)    | O(1)           | O(n)       |
| add(element)  | O(1) amortized | O(1)       |
| add(index)    | O(n)           | O(n)       |
| remove(index) | O(n)           | O(n)       |
| iteration     | Faster         | Slower     |

---

# Why LinkedList Often Performs Worse

People think:

```text id="mnnf6u"
LinkedList is faster for insertion/deletion
```

But in practice:

* locating node takes O(n)
* poor CPU cache locality
* extra memory overhead

So `ArrayList` is usually faster in real applications.

---

# Memory Difference

## ArrayList

Stores only data:

```text id="c4w7ol"
[A][B][C]
```

Efficient memory usage.

---

## LinkedList

Each node stores:

```text id="u6dfw1"
data + next pointer + prev pointer
```

Higher memory overhead.

---

# Cache Locality

## ArrayList

Contiguous memory:

```text id="4ob5j5"
[A][B][C][D]
```

CPU cache friendly ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ faster iteration.

---

# 1. Security

Strings are heavily used in:

* file paths
* network connections


Immutability prevents this.

# 2. String Pool Optimization

Java stores string literals in the:

```text id="9gffg6"

```


* JVM internals

# 1. `char` (Primitive Type)

`char` is a primitive datatype used to store a single character.


# Java Approach Using Two HashMaps

Why two maps?

# Java Code

```java id="jlwm6p"
import java.util.HashMap;

public class IsomorphicStrings {

    public static boolean isIsomorphic(String s, String t) {

        if (s.length() != t.length()) {
            return false;
        }

        HashMap<Character, Character> map1 = new HashMap<>();
        HashMap<Character, Character> map2 = new HashMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {

            char c1 = s.charAt(i);
            char c2 = t.charAt(i);

            // Check s -> t
            if (map1.containsKey(c1)) {
                if (map1.get(c1) != c2) {
                    return false;
                }
            } else {
                map1.put(c1, c2);
            }

            // Check t -> s
            if (map2.containsKey(c2)) {
                if (map2.get(c2) != c1) {
                    return false;
                }
            } else {
                map2.put(c2, c1);
            }
        }

        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        System.out.println(isIsomorphic("egg", "add")); // true
        System.out.println(isIsomorphic("foo", "bar")); // false
    }
}
```
